messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eli, a 39-year-old airline pilot from New Zealand, had always taken pride in his ability to remain calm under pressure. This was a trait that had served him well in his demanding profession. However, following a traumatic incident, he found himself grappling with a reality that felt increasingly unmanageable. The event unfolded one evening while he was off-duty, driving home from a friend’s house. He was stopped at a red light when a police vehicle abruptly pulled up beside him, its sirens blaring. The officers, apparently responding to a nearby altercation, suddenly jumped out of their car. Eli’s heart raced as he witnessed the chaos; he felt a primal fear wash over him as he recalled how an innocent drive had transformed into an overwhelming scene of authority and violence. That night, he felt terror that he had never experienced before, an emotion that clung to him long after the incident.

In the weeks that followed, Eli struggled to shake off the memories of that night. Whenever he found himself in physical proximity to police vehicles, especially during his commutes, a wave of nausea would envelop him. He had come to dread driving with others, certain that the very act of sharing space with another person could lead to another traumatic confrontation. Each time he encountered a police vehicle, the surge of dread that followed felt as real as the danger he had experienced that night, heightening his sense of threat and confirming his fears of chaos lurking around every corner. This heightened sense of threat made the mere presence of police vehicles feel like a warning sign, a reminder of the chaos he had witnessed, igniting a visceral fear that left him feeling trapped. His constant vigilance only served to draw the memories closer, as if the very act of feeling threatened propelled the traumatic recollections to the forefront of his mind, making it impossible for him to escape the past. The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, where even the sight of a police car could send his heart racing and his mind spiraling into worst-case scenarios. Every time he saw a police vehicle, it triggered a wave of anxiety that felt like a confirmation of the danger lurking in the world, reinforcing his belief that he was always at risk of another traumatic event. This fear was compounded by his growing anxiety over delays. When a flight was held up, or traffic slowed unexpectedly, Eli's mind raced with the belief that something sinister was unfolding, a thought rooted in the chaos he had witnessed. Each unexpected delay felt like a confirmation of his fears, reinforcing the notion that danger lurked just around the corner.

Eli’s memories of the traumatic event were vivid and relentless. The intrusive images from that night left him scanning every room he entered, cataloguing exits, and tracking faces, unable to switch off the alertness that had become his new normal. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — like the sound of sirens or the sight of flashing lights — felt like warnings he couldn't afford to ignore, as if they echoed the chaos he had witnessed. Because those memories surfaced so intensely, even ordinary moments, like hearing sirens or seeing flashing lights, became triggers that sent him spiraling back to that night, making him feel as though he was reliving the terror all over again. He often found himself haunted by the recollection of the officers rushing out of their car, an image so real that it eclipsed his ordinary memories. The terror he felt during the incident would seep into his daily life, as mundane moments became tainted with anxiety. Even now, when he tried to recall that night, the experience felt too extreme, too surreal to be a part of his life. He would often catch himself staring into the distance, grappling with the disbelief that he had actually lived through such a harrowing experience. The stark contrast between that night and his regular life further fueled his sense of disconnection.

Eli's sense of threat extended beyond just police interactions. He had begun to feel vulnerable in everyday situations, particularly when encountering strangers. The mere presence of someone approaching him would prompt a visceral response, a fight-or-flight instinct that left him shaken. He felt as if he were constantly on guard, anticipating danger in the most innocuous of encounters. That constant sense of threat kept the traumatic memory alive in his mind, as if he needed to remain vigilant, constantly rehearsing the events to prepare for any potential danger, fueling his anxiety further. This heightened state of alertness was exhausting, and yet Eli felt unable to shake it off, as if acknowledging his fears would somehow make them more real.

The cycle continued to tighten around Eli. His persistent sense of threat kept the traumatic memory alive in his mind, as if he needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever danger might come next. This constant state of alertness made it impossible for him to push the memories away; they surfaced with greater intensity, as if the very act of feeling threatened pulled the recollections from the depths of his mind. His ever-present sense of threat made even the slightest unexpected noise or encounter feel like a signal of impending danger, drawing him back to the memories of that traumatic night, which only deepened his anxiety and avoidance. With his heightened awareness of potential threats, Eli found that even the most mundane stimuli transformed into triggers; every sudden movement or noise felt like an alarm, reaffirming the belief that he was always on the brink of another traumatic experience. The memories of the traumatic event acted as triggers, bringing on a surge of anxiety that made him feel threatened even in safe environments. His heightened sense of threat transformed ordinary stimuli into triggers; every unexpected noise or movement felt like a warning, confirming his belief that he was in constant danger. He would avoid situations that could remind him of the police encounter, fearing that any hint of chaos might send him spiraling back into the nightmare. His avoidance, however, only fed his anxiety. As he distanced himself from the world, it felt as if he were becoming a prisoner in his own mind. His relationships began to suffer; friends and family expressed concern over his increasing withdrawal, yet Eli felt too ashamed to share the extent of his struggles. He had come to believe that admitting his fears would only serve to magnify them, and he was terrified of what that might mean for his future.

Finally, after months of isolation and escalating anxiety, Eli reached a breaking point. A recent flight delay had triggered an overwhelming sense of panic, leading him to pull over on the side of the road, fighting back tears. In that moment, he realized that he could no longer manage his fears alone. The thought of seeking help filled him with trepidation; he was afraid of confronting the memories that haunted him, yet he also felt a flicker of hope that perhaps, with the right support, he could reclaim his life. Eli took a deep breath, recognizing that this step towards seeking help was his first real act of courage since the trauma, and it was a path he was ready to explore.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly convey that triggers directly lead to a sense of threat.
The vignette does not clearly show that memories lead to triggers.
The vignette does not convey that a sense of threat leads to the memory.
The vignette does not show that a sense of threat leads to triggers.
